questions.question: What condition must be fulfilled by a person born outside India after December 3, 2004, to be considered an Indian citizen by descent?

options.text: Both parents must be Indian citizens.
They must reside in India for at least 5 years.
They must renounce any other nationality.
They must reside in India for 10 years.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They must renounce any other nationality**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Indian citizenship is governed by the **Citizenship Act, 1955**, which provides various ways to acquire citizenship, including by **birth**, **descent**, **registration**, and **naturalization**.
 
• For persons born outside **India** on or after **December 3, 2004**, the rules for citizenship by descent were made more stringent by the **Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003**.
 
• Under this amendment, a person born outside the **country** shall not be an Indian citizen unless their birth is registered at an **Indian Consulate** within **one year** of the **date** of birth.
 
• Furthermore, the parents of such a minor must provide a declaration that the child does not hold the **passport of another country**. This essentially means they must not hold (or must effectively **renounce**) any other **nationality** to claim Indian citizenship.
 
• The **Central Government** may, however, allow registration after the expiry of the **one year** period if the parents can show sufficient cause for the delay.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Constitutional Provisions:** **Articles 5 to 11** of **Part II** of the **Constitution of India** deal with citizenship. However, these articles only identified persons who became citizens at the commencement of the Constitution on **January 26, 1950**.
 
• **Citizenship by Birth:**
 
 
• A person born in **India** on or after **January 26, 1950**, but before **July 1, 1987**, is a citizen by birth regardless of the nationality of their parents.
 
• From **July 1, 1987**, to **December 2, 2004**, a person is a citizen only if at least one parent was an Indian citizen at the time of birth.
 
• After **December 3, 2004**, a person born in **India** is a citizen only if both parents are Indian citizens or one is a citizen and the other is not an **illegal migrant**.
 
 
 
• **Citizenship by Registration:** The **Central Government** may register any person (not being an illegal migrant) as a citizen if they belong to categories such as **Persons of Indian Origin (PIO)** who have been ordinarily resident in **India** for **7 years**.
 
• **Citizenship by Naturalization:** A foreigner can acquire Indian citizenship by naturalization if they have resided in **India** for **12 years** (specifically **11 years** in the preceding **14 years** plus the **12 months** immediately preceding the **application**).
 
• **Single Citizenship:** Unlike federal systems like the **USA**, the Indian **Constitution** provides for **single citizenship**, meaning there is no separate state citizenship.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Ministry of Home Affairs** is the nodal **organisation** responsible for matters related to citizenship in **India**.
 
• The **Parliament** derives its power to legislate on citizenship from **Article 11** of the **Constitution**.
 
• **Loss of Citizenship:** The **Citizenship Act, 1955** also prescribes three ways of losing citizenship: **Renunciation** (voluntary), **Termination** (when another country's citizenship is acquired), and **Deprivation** (compulsory termination by the government based on **fraud** or **disloyalty**).
 
• The concept of **Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI)** was introduced to provide certain rights to the **Indian diaspora**, but it does not equate to dual citizenship as **OCI** holders do not have **voting rights** or the right to hold **constitutional posts**.

questions.question: A shopkeeper professes to sell his goods at a 60% loss but uses a false balance and gains 70%. The actual weight (rounded off to one decimal place) that he uses instead of 1 kg is:
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Assume CP of 1 kg = 100

60% loss ⇒ SP (claimed) = 40

70% gain ⇒ Actual SP = 170

⇒ Weight used = (40/170) kg = 0.235 kg

**∴ Answer = 235.3 gm**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Loss claimed = 60%

Actual gain = 70%

**Formula:**

SP = CP × (1 − loss%)

Actual gain ⇒ SP = CP × (1 + profit%)

**Calculation:**

⇒ Let CP of 1 kg = 100

⇒ Claimed SP = 40

⇒ Actual gain 70% ⇒ SP = 170

⇒ Weight used = Claimed SP ÷ Actual SP

⇒ = 40 ÷ 170 = 4/17 ≈ 0.235 kg

∴ Answer = 235.3 gm

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

**False Weight:** Gain = selling less quantity

**Key Idea:** Compare claimed SP with actual SP

**Ratio Trick:** Weight = Claimed ÷ Actual

**Tip:** Assume CP = 100 for speed

⇒ 8x³ − 27y³ = (2x − 3y)(4x² + 6xy + 9y²)

⇒ A=2, B=−3, C=4, D=−9, E=6

⇒ Sum = 2 − 3 + 4 − 9 + 6 = 0

**∴ Answer = 0**

a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²)

**Calculation:**

⇒ 8x³ = (2x)³, 27y³ = (3y)³

⇒ 8x³ − 27y³ = (2x − 3y)(4x² + 6xy + 9y²)

⇒ Compare with (Ax + By)(Cx² − Dy² + Exy)

⇒ A = 2, B = −3

⇒ C = 4, D = −9, E = 6

⇒ A + B + C + D + E = 2 − 3 + 4 − 9 + 6 = 0

**∴ Final Answer = 0**

**Tip:** Always check signs in middle term

questions.question: Which authority is empowered under the Constitution to define the powers, privileges, and immunities of the members of each House of Parliament and their committees?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Parliament itself**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 105** of the **Constitution of India** specifically deals with the powers, privileges, and immunities of the Houses of **Parliament** and their members and committees.
 
• According to **Article 105(3)**, the powers, privileges, and immunities of each House of **Parliament**, and of the members and the committees of each House, shall be such as may from time to time be defined by **Parliament** by law. ***Hence, the statement that Parliament itself is empowered is correct.***
 
• Until so defined by law, these privileges were to be the same as those of the **House of Commons** of the **Parliament of the United Kingdom** as of **January 26, 1950**.
 
• The **44th Amendment Act of 1978** modified this provision to state that the privileges are those which the House, its members, and committees had at the time the amendment came into force, omitting the direct reference to the **British House of Commons**.
 
• While the **Supreme Court** (Option 1) has the power of judicial review to ensure privileges do not violate **Fundamental Rights**, it does not define the privileges themselves. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• The **Speaker of the Lok Sabha** (Option 2) is the guardian of the privileges and decides on matters of breach of privilege within the House but does not have the constitutional authority to "define" them through legislation. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The **President of India** (Option 4) summons the sessions but does not define the legal scope of parliamentary immunities. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Individual Privileges:**

 
 
• **Freedom of Speech:** Under **Article 105(1)**, members have freedom of speech in **Parliament**. No member is liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in **Parliament** or any committee thereof as per **Article 105(2)**.
 
• **Freedom from Arrest:** Members cannot be arrested during the session of **Parliament** and **40 days** before the beginning and **40 days** after the end of a session. This privilege is limited to **civil cases** and does not extend to **criminal cases** or preventive detention.
 
• **Exemption from Jury Service:** Members can refuse to give evidence and appear as a witness in a case pending in a court when **Parliament** is in session.
 
 
 
• **Collective Privileges:**
 
 
• **Right to Publish Proceedings:** The House has the right to publish its reports, debates, and proceedings and can also prohibit others from publishing them.
 
• **Exclusion of Strangers:** Each House has the right to exclude strangers from its proceedings and hold **secret sittings** to discuss important matters.
 
• **Right to Punish:** **Parliament** has the power to punish members as well as outsiders for **breach of privilege** or **contempt of the House** through reprimand, admonition, or imprisonment.
 
• **Inquiry into Proceedings:** The courts are prohibited from inquiring into the proceedings of a House or its committees.
 
 
 
• **State Legislatures:**
 
 
• Similar to **Article 105**, **Article 194** of the **Constitution of India** defines the powers, privileges, and immunities of the **State Legislatures**, their members, and committees.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Codification of Privileges:** To date, **Parliament** has not enacted any comprehensive law to codify all its privileges. They remain based largely on British parliamentary conventions and precedents established over time.
 
• **Privileges vs. Fundamental Rights:** In the **MSM Sharma case (1959)**, the **Supreme Court** held that parliamentary privileges are not subject to **Article 19(1)(a)** (freedom of speech). However, in the **Keshav Singh case (1965)**, the court clarified that privileges are subject to **Article 21** (Right to Life and Personal Liberty).
 
• **Rule of Law:** Despite having vast powers, the exercise of privileges must not be arbitrary and must align with the broader constitutional framework of **India**.

questions.question: If a 7-digit number 56339A8 is completely divisible by 6, what is the minimum value of A?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Divisible by 6 ⇒ divisible by 2 and 3

Last digit = 8 ⇒ divisible by 2 ✔

Sum = 5+6+3+3+9+A+8 = 34 + A

For ÷3 ⇒ (34 + A) multiple of 3

⇒ 34 mod 3 = 1 ⇒ A mod 3 = 2

Smallest A = 2

**∴ Answer = 2**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Number = 56339A8

**Formula:**

Divisible by 6 ⇒ divisible by 2 and 3

**Calculation:**

⇒ Check divisibility by 2:

Last digit = 8 ⇒ divisible ✔

⇒ Check divisibility by 3:

Sum of digits = 5+6+3+3+9+A+8 = 34 + A

⇒ (34 + A) divisible by 3

⇒ 34 ÷ 3 gives remainder 1

⇒ So A must give remainder 2

⇒ Possible A = 2, 5, 8

⇒ Minimum A = 2

**∴ Final Answer = 2**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

**Divisibility by 2:** Last digit even

**Divisibility by 3:** Sum of digits multiple of 3

**Divisibility by 6:** Must satisfy both 2 and 3

**Tip:** Use remainder method for speed

questions.question: The 'Make in India' initiative was launched in which of the following years?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2014**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **'Make in India'** initiative was officially launched by Prime Minister **Narendra Modi** on **September 25, 2014**.
 
• It was designed to facilitate investment, foster innovation, enhance skill development, protect intellectual property, and build best-in-class manufacturing infrastructure in **India**.
 
• The primary goal of the initiative is to transform **India** into a global **design and manufacturing hub**, increasing the **manufacturing sector's** contribution to the **GDP** to **25%** by **2025**.
 
• The logo of **'Make in India'** is a **Lion** made of **gear wheels**, which represents manufacturing, strength, and national pride, reflecting the integral role of the industry in the nation's growth.
 
• Initially, the program targeted **25 economic sectors** for job creation and skill enhancement, including **automobiles**, **aviation**, **biotechnology**, **chemicals**, **defense manufacturing**, **electronic systems**, and **pharmaceuticals**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Four Pillars of Make in India:**

 
 
• **New Processes:** Focuses on **'Ease of Doing Business'** by de-licensing and de-regulating the industry to reduce the complexity of government processes.
 
• **New Infrastructure:** Aims to develop **industrial corridors**, **smart cities**, and state-of-the-art technology to provide modern logistical support.
 
• **New Sectors:** Identification of **25 sectors** in manufacturing, infrastructure, and service activities to provide detailed information and hand-holding for investors.
 
• **New Mindset:** A shift in the government’s role from being a **regulator** to a **facilitator**, partnering with industry to achieve economic growth.
 
 
 
• **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI):** Since the launch in **2014**, the government has liberalized **FDI** norms in several sectors such as **Defense**, **Railways**, **Space**, and **Single Brand Retail Trading** to attract global capital.
 
• **World Bank Rankings:** Due to various reforms under this initiative, **India’s** rank in the **World Bank’s Ease of Doing Business** report improved significantly from **142nd** in **2014** to **63rd** in **2019**.
 
• **National Single Window System (NSWS):** Launched to provide a digital platform to investors for identifying and applying for approvals according to their business requirements, further supporting the **Make in India** vision.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **DPIIT:** The initiative is spearheaded by the **Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)**, which falls under the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry** of the **Government of India**.
 
• **Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme:** To bolster the **Make in India** initiative, the government introduced the **PLI scheme** in **2020** across **14 key sectors** to encourage domestic manufacturing and exports.
 
• **Zero Defect Zero Effect:** A key slogan under the initiative which implies that manufactured goods should have **zero defects** (high quality) and **zero effect** on the environment (sustainability).
 
• **Atmanirbhar Bharat:** Launched in **May 2020**, the **Self-Reliant India** campaign works in tandem with **Make in India** to reduce import dependence and promote **vocal for local**.

questions.question: Three friends X, Y and Z started a business by investing a sum of money in the ratio of 6 : 3 : 5. After 6 months, X withdraws half of his capital. If the sum invested by Z is ₹12,000, then out of a total annual profit of ₹69,000, what is the difference between X's and Y's profit?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Use full ratio (X:Y:Z):

⇒ X effective = 9, Y = 6, Z = 10

Total ratio = 25

⇒ Difference (X−Y) = (9−6)/25 × 69000

⇒ = (3/25) × 69000 = 8280

**∴ Answer = 8280**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

X : Y : Z = 6 : 3 : 5

Z = 12000

X withdraws half after 6 months

Total profit = 69000

**Formula Used:**

Profit ∝ Capital × Time

**Calculation:**

⇒ 5 parts = 12000

⇒ 1 part = 2400

⇒ X = 6 × 2400 = 14400

⇒ Y = 3 × 2400 = 7200

⇒ X for 6 months = 14400 × 6 = 86400

⇒ Remaining X = 7200

⇒ Next 6 months = 7200 × 6 = 43200

⇒ Total X = 129600

⇒ Y for 12 months = 7200 × 12 = 86400

⇒ Z for 12 months = 12000 × 12 = 144000

⇒ Ratio = 129600 : 86400 : 144000

⇒ Divide by 14400 ⇒ 9 : 6 : 10

⇒ Total ratio = 25

⇒ X profit = (9/25) × 69000 = 24840

⇒ Y profit = (6/25) × 69000 = 16560

⇒ Difference = 24840 − 16560 = 8280

**∴ Final Answer = 8280**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

**Profit Sharing:** ∝ Capital × Time

**Withdrawal:** Break into time segments

**Ratio Method:** Convert to simplest ratio

**Tip:** Always include all partners in ratio

questions.question: Which port did the Portuguese capture in 1510, making it their colony’s capital in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Goa**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Portuguese** governor **Afonso de Albuquerque** captured the port of **Goa** in **1510**. He led a successful expedition against the **Sultan of Bijapur**, **Ismail Adil Shah**, to secure a strategic naval base on the western coast of **India**.
 
• Upon its capture, **Goa** became the first Indian territory to be under **European** subordination since the time of **Alexander the Great**. This established **Goa** as a permanent **Portuguese** settlement.
 
• Initially, the **Portuguese** headquarters were located in **Cochin** (Kochi). However, after the capture and consolidation of power, the capital of the **Portuguese State of India** (Estado da Índia) was officially shifted to **Goa** in **1530** by **Nino da Cunha**.
 
• The port of **Goa** was strategically vital for controlling the trade of **Arabian horses** and the export of **spices**, specifically **pepper** and **cinnamon**, to **Europe**.
 
• The **Portuguese** rule in **Goa** lasted for about **450 years**, making it one of the longest colonial possessions in the world. Hence, **Goa** is the correct answer.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Vasco da Gama and Calicut:**

 
 
• The **Portuguese** first arrived in **India** when **Vasco da Gama** reached **Calicut** (Kozhikode) on **May 20, 1498**. He was received by the local ruler known as the **Zamorin**.
 
• While **Calicut** was the entry point, the **Portuguese** faced stiff resistance from **Arab** traders there, which eventually led them to seek other bases like **Goa** and **Cochin**.
 
 
 
• **Francisco de Almeida:**
 
 
• He was appointed as the **first Governor** of the **Portuguese** in **India** in **1505**.
 
• He is famous for the **Blue Water Policy** (Cartaz System), which aimed at making the **Portuguese** the masters of the **Indian Ocean** through naval supremacy rather than land-based forts.
 
 
 
• **Afonso de Albuquerque:**
 
 
• Known as the **Real Founder** of **Portuguese** power in **India**, he succeeded **Almeida** as Governor in **1509**.
 
• He abolished the practice of **Sati** in **Goa** and encouraged **Portuguese** men to marry **Indian** women to create a loyal local population.
 
 
 
• **Other Portuguese Settlements:**
 
 
• Apart from **Goa**, they established colonies in **Daman**, **Diu**, **Salsette**, **Bassein**, and **Chaul**.
 
• The island of **Bombay** (Mumbai) was also under **Portuguese** control until **1661**, when it was given to **King Charles II** of **England** as part of the **dowry** for **Catherine of Braganza**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **End of Portuguese Rule:**

 
 
• **Goa** remained a **Portuguese** colony even after **India** gained independence from the **British** in **1947**.
 
• The **Government of India** launched **Operation Vijay** on **December 18, 1961**, to liberate **Goa**, **Daman**, and **Diu**.
 
• **Goa** was officially integrated into the **Indian Union** on **December 19, 1961**, as a **Union Territory** and later became a full-fledged **State** on **May 30, 1987**.
 
 
 
• **Cultural Impact:**
 
 
• The **Portuguese** introduced the **Printing Press** in **India** at **Goa** in **1556**.
 
• They also introduced new crops to **India**, including **tobacco**, **pineapple**, **cashew**, and **chilli**.

questions.question: The fourth generation of computers marked the use of integrated circuits and compact computing. This generation began with the invention of which key component?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Microprocessor Chip**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **fourth generation** of computers (roughly **1971 to 1980**) is defined by the development and implementation of the **Microprocessor Chip**. • This era saw the transition from **Large Scale Integration** (**LSI**) to **Very Large Scale Integration** (**VLSI**) technology. **VLSI** enabled the placement of hundreds of thousands of **transistors** on a single **microchip**, drastically reducing the **size** and **cost** of computers.

questions.question: What kind of justice do the Directive Principles of State Policy of the Indian Constitution mainly aim to achieve?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Economic and social justice**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)** are enumerated in **Part IV** of the **Constitution of India** under **Articles 36 to 51**.
 
• The main objective of these principles is to establish a **Welfare State** by ensuring **economic and social justice** for all citizens. They serve as guidelines for the **Central** and **State governments** to keep in mind while framing laws and policies. *Hence, option 4 is correct.*
 
• While the **Preamble** mentions **justice—social, economic, and political**, the **DPSP** specifically focuses on providing the socio-economic foundation of a **democracy**. **Political justice** is primarily secured through **Fundamental Rights**, such as the right to vote and equality before the law. *Hence, statement 3 is not the main aim of DPSP alone.*
 
• **Article 37** of the **Constitution** clarifies that these principles are **non-justiciable**, meaning they are not enforceable by any court. However, they are fundamental in the governance of the **country**, and it shall be the duty of the **State** to apply these principles in making laws.
 
• The **DPSP** aims to minimize inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities as per **Article 38**. It seeks to promote the welfare of the people by securing a social order permeated by **social and economic justice**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Source and Background:** The concept of **Directive Principles of State Policy** was borrowed from the **Irish Constitution** of **1937**, which had itself borrowed it from the **Spanish Constitution**. **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** described these principles as **"Novel Features"** of the **Indian Constitution**.
 
• **Classification of DPSP:** Though the **Constitution** does not formally classify them, they are generally grouped into three categories based on their content:
 
 
• **Socialistic Principles:** These aim at providing **social and economic justice**. They direct the state to secure a social order for the welfare of the people (**Article 38**), equal pay for equal work (**Article 39**), and the right to work and education (**Article 41**).
 
• **Gandhian Principles:** These are based on the ideology of **Mahatma Gandhi**. Examples include the organization of **Village Panchayats** (**Article 40**), promotion of cottage industries (**Article 43**), and the prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs (**Article 47**).
 
• **Liberal-Intellectual Principles:** These reflect the ideology of liberalism. Examples include a **Uniform Civil Code** for the citizens (**Article 44**), providing early childhood care and education (**Article 45**), and separation of the **Judiciary** from the **Executive** (**Article 50**).
 
 
 
• **Important Amendments:**
 
 
• The **42nd Amendment Act of 1976** added four new principles: **Article 39** (opportunities for healthy development of children), **Article 39A** (equal justice and free legal aid), **Article 43A** (participation of workers in management), and **Article 48A** (protection of environment).
 
• The **86th Amendment Act of 2002** changed the subject of **Article 45** and made elementary education a **Fundamental Right** under **Article 21A**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights vs. DPSP:** While **Fundamental Rights** (Part III) protect individual liberties and provide **political justice**, the **DPSP** (Part IV) promote the collective well-being and provide **economic and social justice**. In the **Minerva Mills Case (1980)**, the **Supreme Court** held that the **Indian Constitution** is founded on the bedrock of the balance between **Part III** and **Part IV**.
 
• **Implementation:** Several laws have been enacted to implement **DPSP**, such as the **Minimum Wages Act (1948)**, the **Maternity Benefit Act (1961)**, and the **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA)** of **2005**.
 
• **International Peace:** **Article 51** specifically directs the **State** to promote international peace and security and maintain just and honorable relations between **nations**.

questions.question: Which feature of the 10th-century CE Lingaraja Temple in Bhubaneswar reflects the Nagara architectural style?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Curvilinear shikhara tower**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Lingaraja Temple**, located in **Bhubaneswar**, **Odisha**, is one of the most prominent examples of the **Kalinga** style of architecture, which is a sub-type of the broader **Nagara** architectural style.
 
• Built primarily in the **11th Century CE**, the temple is dedicated to **Lord Shiva** (worshipped as **Harihara**) and was largely constructed by the **Somavamsi dynasty**, with later additions by the **Ganga rulers**.
 
• A defining feature of the **Nagara** style is the **Shikhara** (mountain peak), and in the case of the Lingaraja Temple, it features a massive **Curvilinear shikhara tower**. This tower, known as **Rekha Deula**, rises to a height of about **55 meters** (**180 feet**).
 
• The temple complex is structured into four distinct components: the **Garbhagriha** (sanctum sanctorum), the **Jagamohana** (assembly hall), the **Natamandira** (festival/dance hall), and the **Bhoga-mandapa** (hall of offerings).
 
• The **Curvilinear shikhara** is topped with an **Amalaka** (a ribbed stone disk) and a **Kalasha** (finial), which are quintessential elements of the **Nagara** tradition in **North India**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Nagara Architectural Style:**

 
 
• Originating in **North India**, this style is characterized by a **cruciform plan** and a **curvilinear tower**.
 
• Unlike **South Indian** temples, **Nagara** temples typically do not have elaborate **boundary walls** or massive **gateways** (Gopurams).
 
 
 
• **Stepped pyramid vimana:**
 
 
• This feature is characteristic of the **Dravidian** style of architecture found in **South India**, where the tower (Vimana) rises in a series of **diminishing tiers**. While **Kalinga** architecture uses "**Pidha Deula**" (stepped roofs) for assembly halls, the main sanctum's tower in Nagara style is curvilinear. *Hence, this statement is incorrect regarding the primary Nagara reflective feature.*
 
 
 
• **Circular stupa dome:**
 
 
• The **Stupa** is a core element of **Buddhist architecture**, such as the **Great Stupa at Sanchi**. It is a hemispherical mound used to house relics and is not a feature of **Hindu Nagara** temple towers. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
 
 
• **Ornate gopuram entrance:**
 
 
• **Gopurams** are the monumental, highly decorated entrance towers typical of **Dravidian architecture** (e.g., **Meenakshi Temple** in **Madurai**). In **Nagara** style, the entrance is usually less emphasized than the main **Shikhara**. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context:** The construction is often attributed to **King Jajati Keshari** of the **Soma Dynasty** and was completed by his son **Lalatendu Keshari**.
 
• **Materials:** The temple is built using **dark red sandstone** and **laterite**, which were locally available in **Odisha**.
 
• **Significance:** **Bhubaneswar** is often referred to as the "**Ekambra Kshetra**" or the "**Temple City of India**" due to the density of these **medieval** structures.
 
• **Cultural Impact:** The **Lingaraja Temple** set the benchmark for subsequent **Odishan** temples, including the world-famous **Jagannath Temple** in **Puri** and the **Sun Temple** at **Konark** (built in the **13th Century CE**).
 
• **Iconography:** The exterior walls are decorated with intricate **sculptures** of **Gods**, **Goddesses**, **musical instruments**, and **secular scenes**, representing the peak of **Odishan artistic** excellence.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT correct about the scheme of Jan Shikshan Sansthan of the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE)?

options.text: It focuses on creation of a pool of master trainers
It is implemented through Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs)
It focuses to improve the occupational skills and technical knowledge of the non/neo literates and persons having rudimentary level of education

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It is implemented through Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1:** The **Jan Shikshan Sansthan (JSS)** scheme emphasizes the **creation of a pool of master trainers** and **resource persons** who are skilled in specific vocations to provide training at the **grassroots level**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 2:** The **JSS** scheme is not implemented through **Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs)**; instead, it is implemented through **Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs)** and **voluntary agencies** registered under the **Societies Registration Act, 1860**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Statement 3:** The primary objective of the scheme is to improve the **occupational skills** and **technical knowledge** of **non-literates**, **neo-literates**, and persons with a **rudimentary level of education** (up to **8th standard**) and **school dropouts** (up to **12th standard**). ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 4:** The scheme focuses on identifying and promoting **traditional skills** in the **districts** through **skilling** and **upskilling**, ensuring that local heritage and indigenous crafts provide **livelihood opportunities**. ***Hence, statement 4 is correct.***
 
• The **Jan Shikshan Sansthan** scheme is a unique initiative that aims to provide **vocational training** in a **non-formal** mode to the marginalized sections of society.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Historical Background:** The scheme was initially launched as **Shramik Vidyapeeth** in the **year 1967** in **Mumbai**. It was later renamed **Jan Shikshan Sansthan** in the **year 2000**.
 
• **Institutional Transfer:** The scheme was previously under the **Ministry of Human Resource Development (MHRD)**, but it was transferred to the **Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE)** in **July 2018** to better align vocational training with **market demands**.
 
• **Target Demographics:** The priority group for **JSS** includes **women**, **Scheduled Castes (SC)**, **Scheduled Tribes (ST)**, **minorities**, and other **economically weaker sections**. The **age group** of the target beneficiaries is usually **15 to 45 years**.
 
• **Geographical Reach:** There are approximately **301** functional **Jan Shikshan Sansthans** spread across various **districts** in **India**, serving both **rural** and **urban** slum areas.
 
• **Course Varieties:** The training includes a wide range of trades such as **cutting and tailoring**, **beauty culture and health care**, **electrical technician**, **soft toys making**, and **handicrafts**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Funding Structure:** **JSS** is a **100% Central Sector Scheme**. The **Government of India** provides an annual recurring grant to the **NGOs** for **infrastructure**, **staff salaries**, and **training expenses**.
 
• **Certification:** Trainees receive a **certificate** upon successful completion of the course, which is often validated by the **National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET)**, improving their chances for **self-employment** or **wage employment**.
 
• **Digital Literacy:** In recent years, the **MSDE** has integrated **digital literacy** and **life skills** into the **JSS** curriculum to ensure that beneficiaries can navigate the modern **digital economy** and access **government schemes**.
 
• **Impact and Monitoring:** The performance of each **Sansthan** is monitored through a dedicated **JSS Portal**, which tracks **enrollment**, **training progress**, and **placement data** of the candidates.

questions.question: The e/m ratio for electron was determined by:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**J.J. Thomson**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **e/m ratio**, which represents the **charge-to-mass ratio** of an electron, was first determined by the **British physicist J.J. Thomson** in the year **1897**.
 
• Thomson utilized a **Cathode Ray Tube (CRT)** experiment to measure the deflection of cathode rays under the simultaneous application of **electric and magnetic fields**.
 
• He observed that the amount of deviation of the particles from their path in the presence of an electrical or magnetic field depends upon the **magnitude of the negative charge** on the particle, the **mass of the particle**, and the **strength of the magnetic or electric field**.
 
• By balancing the transverse electric and magnetic fields, he was able to calculate the velocity of the particles and subsequently determine the **specific charge (e/m)** of the electron.
 
• The value determined for the **e/m ratio** of an electron is approximately **1.758820 × 10¹¹ C/kg** (Coulombs per kilogram).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Albert Einstein:** He is renowned for his theory of **relativity** and the **mass-energy equivalence formula (E=mc²)**. In **1905**, he explained the **Photoelectric Effect**, which provided crucial evidence for the **quantization of light** (photons), for which he received the **Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921**.
 
• **Niels Bohr:** A **Danish physicist** who proposed the **Bohr Model of the atom** in **1913**. He introduced the idea that electrons move in **fixed orbits (energy levels)** around the nucleus and that **angular momentum** is quantized. His work was fundamental to **quantum mechanics**.
 
• **Issac Newton:** An **English mathematician and physicist** who formulated the **Laws of Motion** and the **Universal Law of Gravitation**. His work, **Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica**, published in **1687**, laid the foundation for **classical mechanics**.
 
• **J.J. Thomson's Plum Pudding Model:** Following his discovery of the electron, Thomson proposed that an atom is a sphere of **positive electrification** in which **negatively charged electrons** are embedded like seeds in a watermelon or raisins in a pudding.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Millikan’s Oil Drop Experiment:** While Thomson found the **ratio**, the actual **charge (e)** of an electron was determined by **R.A. Millikan** in **1909**. He found the charge to be **-1.6022 × 10⁻¹⁹ Coulombs**.
 
• **Mass of Electron:** By combining Thomson's **e/m ratio** and Millikan's **charge (e)**, the **mass (m)** of the electron was calculated to be **9.1094 × 10⁻³¹ kg**.
 
• **Nature of Cathode Rays:** Thomson concluded that **cathode rays** consist of negatively charged particles, which he called "corpuscles," later named **electrons**. He also found that the **e/m ratio** was independent of the **nature of the gas** or the **material of the electrodes** used in the discharge tube, proving that electrons are basic constituents of all atoms.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT belong to the Tibeto-Burman language family?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Assamese**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Assamese** is an **Indo-Aryan** language spoken primarily in the state of **Assam**. It serves as the **lingua franca** of the region and is the easternmost **Indo-Aryan** language, having developed from **Magadhi Prakrit**. Since it belongs to the **Indo-European** family rather than the **Sino-Tibetan** family, it does not belong to the **Tibeto-Burman** group. ***Hence, the statement regarding Assamese is correct.***
 
• **Lepcha** is a language spoken by the **Lepcha people** in **Sikkim** and the **Darjeeling** district of **West Bengal**. It is a member of the **Tibeto-Burman** language family, which is a subgroup of the larger **Sino-Tibetan** family. ***Hence, the statement regarding Lepcha is incorrect.***
 
• **Bodo** (also known as **Boro**) is an official language of the state of **Assam** and is part of the **Bodo-Koch** group of the **Tibeto-Burman** language family. It is predominantly spoken by the **Bodo community** in **Northeast India**. ***Hence, the statement regarding Bodo is incorrect.***
 
• **Garo** is a language spoken by the **Garo people**, mainly in the **Garo Hills** of **Meghalaya**, as well as in parts of **Assam** and **Bangladesh**. It is closely related to the **Bodo** language and falls under the **Bodo-Garo** subfamily of the **Tibeto-Burman** languages. ***Hence, the statement regarding Garo is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Indo-Aryan Language Family:** This family includes major languages of **Northern** and **Central India** such as **Hindi**, **Bengali**, **Punjabi**, **Marathi**, **Gujarati**, and **Assamese**. These languages are descendants of **Old Indo-Aryan** (**Sanskrit**). **Assamese** specifically uses a script that is almost identical to the **Bengali script**, with a few minor variations.
 
• **Tibeto-Burman Language Family:** This is a massive group of languages spoken across **Southeast Asia**, **China**, and the **Himalayan** regions. In **India**, these languages are prevalent in the **Seven Sister States** (Northeast) and **Ladakh**. Examples include **Manipuri** (Meitei), **Mizo**, **Angami**, and **Adi**.
 
• **Linguistic Diversity of Northeast India:** The region is a "linguistic mosaic" where three major language families meet: **Indo-Aryan** (Assamese, Sylheti), **Sino-Tibetan/Tibeto-Burman** (Bodo, Garo, Naga languages), and **Austroasiatic** (Khasi, Jaintia).
 
• **Geographical Distribution:** While **Assamese** is concentrated in the **Brahmaputra Valley**, **Tibeto-Burman** languages are typically found in the surrounding **hilly terrains**. For instance, **Garo** is prominent in the **western part** of **Meghalaya**, and **Lepcha** is found in the **high-altitude** regions of the **Eastern Himalayas**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Constitutional Status:** Both **Assamese** and **Bodo** are recognized in the **Eighth Schedule** of the **Constitution of India**. **Assamese** was included in the original list in **1950**, whereas **Bodo** was added through the **92nd Amendment Act** in **2003**.
 
• **Classical Language Status:** In **October 2024**, the **Union Cabinet** of **India** approved the conferment of **Classical Language** status to **Assamese**, along with **Marathi**, **Pali**, **Prakrit**, and **Bengali**, recognizing its ancient literary heritage.
 
• **Language Characteristics:** **Tibeto-Burman** languages are often **tonal** (like **Bodo**) or have complex **agglutinative** structures. In contrast, **Assamese** is an **inflected** language, similar to other **Indo-European** languages, though it has been significantly influenced by the surrounding **Sino-Tibetan** phonology and vocabulary over **centuries**.
 
• **Demographics:** According to the **2011 Census**, **Assamese** is spoken by over **15 million** people, making it the most widely spoken language in **Northeast India**. **Bodo** has approximately **1.4 million** speakers, and **Garo** has about **1.1 million** speakers in **India**.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the Control Unit (CU) within the Central Processing Unit (CPU)?

options.text: It performs all the arithmetic and logical calculations on data.
It manages and coordinates the flow of instructions and data throughout the computer system.
It provides the system's primary volatile storage for active programs.
It permanently stores the operating system and basic boot instructions.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It manages and coordinates the flow of instructions and data throughout the computer system.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Control Unit (CU)** is a core component of the **Central Processing Unit (CPU)** that directs the operation of the processor. It essentially acts as the "manager" or "brain" of the CPU, ensuring all components work in harmony.
 
• Its primary **function** is to **manage and coordinate** the movement of data and instructions between the **CPU**, **Main Memory**, and various **Input/Output (I/O) devices**.
 
• The **Control Unit** does not execute the data processing itself; instead, it issues **timing and control signals** to other units, such as the **Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)** and **Registers**, telling them what to do.
 
• It is responsible for the **Instruction Cycle**, which includes **fetching** an instruction from memory, **decoding** it to understand the required operation, and **executing** it by routing signals to the appropriate hardware components.
 
• By interpreting the **machine code** or **assembly language** instructions, the **CU** ensures that the hardware performs the correct sequence of steps for any given software program.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU):**

 
 
• This component performs all **arithmetic calculations** (like **addition**, **subtraction**, **multiplication**, and **division**) and **logical comparisons** (such as **AND**, **OR**, **NOT**, and **equal to**).
 
• While the **Control Unit** directs the flow, the **ALU** is the part of the **CPU** where the actual mathematical "work" is completed. *Hence, option 1 describes the ALU and is incorrect.*
 
 
 
• **Random Access Memory (RAM):**
 
 
• **RAM** serves as the system's **primary volatile storage**. It holds the **data** and **active programs** currently in use by the **CPU**.
 
• It is called **volatile** because all stored information is lost when the **power** is turned off. *Hence, option 3 describes RAM and is incorrect.*
 
 
 
• **Read-Only Memory (ROM) and Hard Drives:**
 
 
• **ROM** stores **permanent instructions** such as the **BIOS (Basic Input/Output System)**, which are necessary to **boot** the computer.
 
• **Hard Disk Drives (HDD)** or **Solid State Drives (SSD)** provide **non-volatile storage** for the **Operating System** and user files. *Hence, option 4 describes permanent storage devices and is incorrect.*
 
 
 
• **Registers:**
 
 
• These are small, **high-speed storage locations** inside the **CPU**. They hold **immediate data**, **addresses**, and **instructions** that are being processed at that very microsecond.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Types of Control Units:** There are generally two types of **Control Units**. The **Hardwired CU** uses **fixed logic circuits** (like **gates** and **flip-flops**) and is extremely **fast**. The **Microprogrammed CU** uses a **control store** to hold **micro-instructions**, making it more **flexible** and easier to design but slightly slower.
 
• **Program Counter (PC):** This is a special **register** used by the **Control Unit** to keep track of the **memory address** of the **next instruction** to be processed.
 
• **System Clock:** The **Control Unit** relies on the **System Clock** to synchronize all internal operations. The speed at which the **CU** can process instructions is often measured in **Gigahertz (GHz)**.
 
• **Control Bus:** The **CU** communicates with other hardware via the **Control Bus**, sending signals that specify whether a **read** or **write** operation is being performed on the **memory** or **I/O devices**.

questions.question: Akhaj Mesolithic site is found in which state of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gujarat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Akhaj** is a prominent **Mesolithic** archaeological site located in the **Mehsana** district of **Gujarat**, India.
 
• The site is part of the **Langhnaj** cultural complex, situated within the **sandy plains** of the **Sabarmati** river basin, which is known for its rich density of prehistoric settlements.
 
• It represents the **Middle Stone Age** (Mesolithic) culture, a period characterized by a shift in human lifestyle toward more specialized **hunting-gathering** and the early stages of **sedentism**.
 
• Findings at **Akhaj** include a significant collection of **microliths**, which are tiny, sharp stone tools made from materials like **chert**, **agate**, and **chalcedony**, used for hunting and domestic activities.
 
• Archaeological excavations in this region have provided evidence of various animal remains, such as **wild cattle**, **deer**, and **boar**, suggesting a diverse diet and an environment that supported a wide range of fauna during the **Holocene** epoch.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Mesolithic Period in India:**

 
 
• The **Mesolithic** era in **India** generally dates from approximately **10,000 BCE** to **4,000 BCE**. It serves as a vital bridge between the **Palaeolithic** (Old Stone Age) and the **Neolithic** (New Stone Age).
 
• This period is marked by a transition in climate to warmer and more **humid** conditions following the end of the last **Ice Age**, leading to changes in flora and fauna.
 
 
 
• **Geographical Distribution:**
 
 
• Apart from **Gujarat**, significant Mesolithic sites are found across **India**, including **Bagor** in **Rajasthan** (one of the largest Mesolithic sites), **Adamgarh** in **Madhya Pradesh**, and **Sarai Nahar Rai** in **Uttar Pradesh**.
 
• In **Gujarat**, other notable sites include **Loteshwar** and **Ratanpur**, which provide evidence of very early **animal domestication**, particularly **sheep** and **goats**.
 
 
 
• **Tool Technology:**
 
 
• The defining feature of this period is **microlithic** technology. These tools were often **geometric** in shape, such as **crescents**, **triangles**, and **trapezes**, and were frequently **hafted** onto wooden or bone handles to make composite tools like arrows or sickles.
 
 
 
• **Socio-Cultural Evolution:**
 
 
• During the later Mesolithic phases at sites like **Akhaj**, humans began to use **handmade pottery**, indicating an evolution in storage and cooking techniques.
 
• There is also evidence of **rock art** and **paintings** from this period (most famously at **Bhimbetka**), which depict scenes of hunting, dancing, and social life.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of H.D. Sankalia:** The archaeological landscape of **Gujarat** was extensively studied by the renowned archaeologist **H.D. Sankalia** between **1941** and **1963**. His work at **Langhnaj** (near **Akhaj**) was pioneering in establishing the sequence of the **Mesolithic** culture in **Western India**.
 
• **Burial Practices:** Excavations at **Mesolithic** sites in **Gujarat** have unearthed human **skeletons**. The **burials** were typically in a **flexed** or crouched position, often with the head facing **West**, and sometimes included **grave goods** like bone ornaments or stone tools, reflecting early ritualistic behaviors.
 
• **Environmental Adaptation:** The people of **Akhaj** lived on **sand dunes** (fossilized dunes) located near **oxbow lakes** or rivers, demonstrating a strategic choice of **location** to ensure access to water and diverse food resources.

• **Primitive Subsistence Farming** is still practiced in certain pockets of **India** on small patches of land. It utilizes **traditional tools** such as the **hoe**, **dao**, and **digging sticks**, and relies heavily on **family or community labor**.

• Both **Bryophytes** and **Algae** contain **chlorophyll** and are **photoautotrophic**, meaning they can **prepare their own food**. Since both groups share this **feature**, it does not serve as a differentiating factor. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• **Cryptogams** are plants that reproduce via **spores** rather than **seeds**. This category includes **Thallophyta (Algae)**, **Bryophyta**, and **Pteridophyta**. Because both belong to this **classification**, it is not a point of difference. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• The possession of **chlorophyll** is a fundamental **characteristic** of almost all green plants, including all **Algae** and **Bryophytes**. It allows them to perform **photosynthesis** to sustain growth. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• In **Algae**, the **zygote** is usually released from the parent plant or undergoes **meiosis** directly without forming a multicellular **embryo** stage, which is the key **evolutionary** advancement seen in **Bryophytes**.

• **Bryophytes (The Amphibians of the Plant Kingdom):**

 
 
• **Location and Habitat:** They are found in **moist, shady, and humid localities**. They are called **amphibians** because they live on **land** but require **water** for **fertilization** (for the movement of **flagellated antherozoids**).
 
• **Structure:** The **plant body** is more differentiated than that of **algae**. It is **thallus-like** and prostrate or erect, attached to the **substratum** by unicellular or multicellular **rhizoids**. They lack **true roots, stems, or leaves**.
 
• **Life Cycle:** The dominant phase of the life cycle is the **haploid gametophyte**. The **sporophyte** is physically dependent on the **gametophyte** for **nutrition**.
 
• **Examples:** Common examples include **Marchantia** (Liverwort), **Funaria** (Moss), and **Anthoceros** (Hornwort).
 
 
 
• **Algae (Thallophyta):**
 
 
• **Features:** They are **chlorophyll-bearing**, simple, **thalloid**, and largely **aquatic** (both **freshwater** and **marine**) organisms.
 
• **Classification:** Based on **pigmentation**, they are divided into **Chlorophyceae** (Green algae), **Phaeophyceae** (Brown algae), and **Rhodophyceae** (Red algae).
 
• **Functions:** They are the primary **producers** of **energy-rich compounds** in **aquatic ecosystems** and are responsible for at least **half of the total carbon dioxide fixation** on **Earth**.
 
• **Uses:** Many species like **Porphyra**, **Laminaria**, and **Sargassum** are used as **food**, while others produce **hydrocolloids** like **algin** and **carrageenan**.

• **Sex Organs:** In **Bryophytes**, the **sex organs** (**Antheridium** and **Archegonium**) are **multicellular** and protected by a **sterile jacket** of cells. In **Algae**, **sex organs** are typically **unicellular** and lack a **protective jacket** (except in **Chara**).
 
• **Vascular Tissue:** Both **Algae** and **Bryophytes** lack **vascular tissues** like **xylem** and **phloem**, which is why they generally remain **small in size**. The **evolution** of **vascular tissue** first occurred in **Pteridophytes**.
 
• **Ecological Importance:** **Bryophytes** play a **significant role** in **plant succession** on **bare rocks** and **soil**, helping in the **formation of soil** and **preventing erosion**.

questions.question: In an election between two candidates, 80% of the registered voters cast their vote and 15% of the votes polled were found invalid. Winning candidate got 75% of the valid votes and won the election by a margin of 289 votes. How many voters were registered?

Valid votes = 80% × 85% = 68% of N

Winning margin = (75% − 25%) = 50% of valid

⇒ Margin = 50% of 68% = 34% of N

⇒ 0.34N = 289 ⇒ N = 850

**∴ Answer = 850**

Votes cast = 80%

Invalid votes = 15%

Winner gets 75%

Margin = 289

⇒ Winner votes = 75% of 0.68N = 0.51N

⇒ Loser votes = 25% of 0.68N = 0.17N

⇒ Margin = 0.51N − 0.17N = 0.34N

**∴ Total voters = 850**

• The **Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS)**, headquartered in **Tashkent, Uzbekistan**, is a permanent organ of the **SCO** which promotes cooperation of member states against **terrorism, separatism, and extremism**.

questions.question: The modified petiole of Acacia species that resembles a leaf blade is termed as __________________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**phyllode**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **phyllode** is a specialized **modified petiole** or a portion of the **leaf rachis** that becomes flattened, green, and leaf-like in appearance and function. In certain plants, especially the **Australian Acacia** (such as **Acacia auriculiformis**), the true leaves are **bipinnately compound** but fall off very early in the plant's life cycle (deciduous).
 
• The primary **function** of a phyllode is to carry out **photosynthesis**, a role typically performed by the leaf blade (lamina). Because these plants often grow in **arid** or **xerophytic** environments, this modification helps in reducing **transpiration**.
 
• Phyllodes are usually oriented **vertically**. This specific **feature** allows them to avoid the direct impact of the intense **midday sun**, thereby reducing heat absorption and water loss, which is a critical **adaptation** for survival in dry climates.
 
• Morphologically, the **phyllode** can be distinguished from a true leaf by the absence of a **leaf blade** and its origin from the **petiole**. It contains **chlorophyll** and possesses **stomata**, though they are often fewer in **number** compared to regular leaves to conserve moisture. ***Hence, the statement regarding the modified petiole in Acacia is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Spines**:

 
 
• These are hard, **pointed structures** that represent modified leaves, stipules, or parts of leaves.
 
• Their primary **function** is to provide **protection** against **herbivores** and to reduce the surface area for **transpiration** in **desert** plants.
 
• **Examples** include the spines found in **Cactus** (Opuntia), where the entire leaf is modified into a spine, or **Ziziphus**, where stipules become spines.
 
 
 
• **Tendrils**:
 
 
• These are thin, **thread-like**, sensitive structures used by **climbing plants** for **support**.
 
• In some species, the entire leaf is modified into a tendril (e.g., **Wild Pea** or **Lathyrus aphaca**), while in others, only the leaflets are modified (e.g., **Garden Pea** or **Pisum sativum**).
 
• They exhibit **thigmotropism**, meaning they coil around any object they come into **contact** with to help the plant climb.
 
 
 
• **Bracts**:
 
 
• These are modified leaves associated with **reproductive structures** like flowers or **inflorescences**.
 
• While they often look like small green scales, in plants like **Bougainvillea**, they are **brightly colored** to attract **pollinators** such as insects and birds.
 
• They are located at the **base** of the flower pedicel or the main axis of the inflorescence.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• It is important to distinguish a **phyllode** from a **phylloclade**. While a phyllode is a modified **petiole** (leaf part), a **phylloclade** is a modified **stem** (e.g., **Opuntia**) that performs photosynthesis and stores water.
 
• The **location** of most **Acacia** species with phyllodes is **Australia**, where they have evolved to thrive in **nutrient-poor** and **water-stressed** soils.
 
• The **year 1860** and onwards saw significant botanical documentation of these species by **taxonomists** like **George Bentham**, who categorized them based on these unique **morphological features**.
 
• In the context of **India**, the **Australian Acacia** (Acacia auriculiformis) is widely used in **social forestry** and **afforestation** programs due to its fast growth and **adaptability** to degraded lands.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a primary air pollutant?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ozone**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Primary pollutants** are those that are emitted **directly** into the atmosphere from a source, such as **volcanoes**, **industrial stacks**, or **vehicle exhausts**.
 
• **Sulfur dioxide (SO2)** is a **primary pollutant** primarily produced from the **combustion of fossil fuels** (like **coal** and **oil**) and **industrial processes** such as **smelting**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect in the context of the question.***
 
• **Carbon monoxide (CO)** is a **colorless, odorless gas** that is a **primary pollutant**, emitted directly from the **incomplete combustion** of **carbon-based fuels** in **motor vehicles** and **power plants**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect in the context of the question.***
 
• **Nitrogen oxides (NOx)**, specifically **Nitrogen dioxide (NO2)** and **Nitric oxide (NO)**, are **primary pollutants** produced during **high-temperature combustion** in **car engines** and **factories**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect in the context of the question.***
 
• **Ozone (O3)** is **not emitted directly** into the air; instead, it is a **secondary pollutant** formed by **chemical reactions** between **Nitrogen oxides (NOx)** and **Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs)** in the presence of **sunlight**. ***Hence, statement 4 is correct as it is NOT a primary pollutant.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Secondary Air Pollutants:**

 
 
• These are not emitted directly but form when **primary pollutants** react in the **atmosphere**.
 
• Key examples include **Ozone (O3)**, **Peroxyacetyl Nitrate (PAN)**, **Sulfuric acid (H2SO4)**, and **Nitric acid (HNO3)**.
 
• **Photochemical Smog** is a mixture of **primary and secondary pollutants**, primarily composed of **ground-level ozone**.
 
 
 
• **Ground-level Ozone vs. Stratospheric Ozone:**
 
 
• **Tropospheric (ground-level) Ozone** is a **harmful air pollutant** that affects **human health** and **vegetation**.
 
• **Stratospheric Ozone** (the **Ozone Layer**) is "good" ozone located **10 to 50 km** above the Earth, protecting life from **Ultraviolet (UV) radiation**.
 
 
 
• **Air Pollution Control in India:**
 
 
• The **Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act** was enacted in **1981** to combat air pollution.
 
• The **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)** monitors air quality through the **National Air Quality Index (AQI)**, which tracks **eight major pollutants** including **PM10**, **PM2.5**, **NO2**, **SO2**, **CO**, **O3**, **NH3**, and **Pb (Lead)**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Particulate Matter (PM):** These are **primary pollutants** categorized by size. **PM2.5** refers to particles smaller than **2.5 micrometers**, which can penetrate deep into the **lungs** and **bloodstream**.
 
• **Acid Rain:** It is a result of **secondary pollutants**. When **Sulfur dioxide** and **Nitrogen oxides** react with **water vapor** in the air, they form **sulfuric** and **nitric acids**, falling as **acidic precipitation** with a **pH lower than 5.6**.
 
• **Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs):** These are **organic chemicals** (like **benzene** and **formaldehyde**) that have a **high vapor pressure** at room temperature. They are crucial precursors to the formation of **ozone**.
 
• **National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS):** In **India**, **NAAQS** are the standards for ambient air quality set by the **CPCB** to protect **public health** and the **environment** from the harmful effects of air pollution.

questions.question: Restarting a computer means:

options.text: Turning it off and on again automatically

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Turning it off and on again automatically**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Restarting**, also known as **rebooting**, is the process by which a running **computer system** is closed and then started again. This process involves the **Operating System** (OS) closing all **applications**, clearing the **RAM**, and then reloading the **system software** and **drivers**.
 
• **Only refreshing the desktop** refers to a manual action (typically using the **F5 key** or **Right-click > Refresh**) that reloads the icons and **graphical user interface** (GUI) without affecting running **background processes** or the **hardware state**. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Turning it off permanently** refers to a **Shutdown** operation, where the **power supply** is cut off and the **CPU** stops processing entirely until a user manually presses the **physical power button**. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Installing a new OS** is a complex process called a **clean installation** or **upgrade**, which involves rewriting the **hard drive** or **SSD** data. While it requires **restarts**, the act of restarting itself is not the same as an **installation**. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Turning it off and on again automatically** is the standard **function** of a **restart** command in modern **computing**. The system shuts down the **software environment** and triggers the **BIOS/UEFI** to initiate the **boot sequence** immediately. *Hence, this statement is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Booting:**

 
 
• **Cold Booting:** This occurs when a **computer** is started from a completely powered-off state. It involves the **Power-on Self-test** (**POST**) which checks the **integrity** of the **hardware** like **RAM**, **CPU**, and **Storage**.
 
• **Warm Booting:** This is a **restart** initiated while the **computer** is already on. It is typically faster than a **cold boot** because it might skip some **hardware diagnostic tests** performed by the **BIOS**.
 
 
 
• **Functions and Benefits:**
 
 
• **Clearing Memory:** A **restart** clears the **Random Access Memory** (**RAM**), which removes **temporary files**, **cached data**, and **memory leaks** caused by poorly coded **applications**.
 
• **Software Updates:** Many **Security Patches** and **OS updates** require a **restart** to replace **system files** that are currently in use by the **Operating System**.
 
• **Troubleshooting:** It is the primary step in **IT Support** to resolve **system freezes**, **peripheral connectivity issues**, and **network errors**.
 
 
 
• **Power States:**
 
 
• **Sleep Mode:** Keeps the **current session** in **RAM** and uses a small amount of **power** for instant **resumption**.
 
• **Hibernation:** Saves the **RAM** state to the **hard disk** and turns off the **power** completely.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **BIOS/UEFI Role:** When a **restart** occurs, the **Basic Input/Output System** (**BIOS**) or the modern **Unified Extensible Firmware Interface** (**UEFI**) takes control to identify and initialize **system hardware** before handing off control back to the **Bootloader**.
 
• **History:** In **older computers** (pre-**1990s**), a **restart** often required a **physical reset button**. In **modern systems**, the **ACPI** (Advanced Configuration and Power Interface) allows the **OS** to manage **power states** and **automatic restarts** seamlessly.
 
• **Data Integrity:** Performing a **proper restart** via the **menu** (Soft Reset) is always safer than a **Hard Reset** (unplugging **power**), as it allows the **disk** to finish **write operations** and prevents **file system corruption**.

• **Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance:**

• **R21 vs. RTS,S:** While **RTS,S** (known as **Mosquirix**) was the first vaccine to be approved in **2021**, the **R21** vaccine (approved in **October 2023**) is easier to manufacture at scale and is significantly cheaper, which is vital for mass immunization programs.
 
• **Funding Mechanism:** The procurement of these vaccines is supported by **Gavi’s** funding window for malaria vaccines, which was approved by the **Gavi Board** in **December 2021**.
 
• **Serum Institute of India (SII):** Based in **Pune**, **India**, **SII** is the world's largest vaccine manufacturer by number of doses produced and sold globally. Their involvement is key to the **"Make in India"** initiative and global health security.

questions.question: Which of the following leader is associated with the founding of the Brahmo Samaj and its emphasis on monotheism and social reform?

__
 
• **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** founded the **Brahmo Sabha** in **August 1828**, which was later renamed the **Brahmo Samaj**. It was one of the first socio-religious reform movements in **India** aimed at purging **Hinduism** of its social evils and superstitions.
 
• He was a strong proponent of **monotheism** and believed in the worship of one **Supreme God**. To promote this, he published **Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin** (A Gift to Monotheists) in **1803** and translated the **Upanishads** into **Bengali** to prove that ancient Hindu texts supported **monotheism**.
 
• One of his most significant social reforms was the agitation against the practice of **Sati**. His relentless efforts led the then **Governor-General Lord William Bentinck** to pass the **Sati Regulation Act** in **1829**, which declared the practice illegal and punishable by law.
 
• He advocated for **women's rights**, including the right of **widows to remarry** and the right of **women to hold property**. He vehemently opposed **polygamy** and the **caste system**, arguing for a more egalitarian society.
 
• In the field of education, he supported **Western science** and **English education**. He collaborated with **David Hare** to establish the **Hindu College** in **Calcutta** (now **Kolkata**) in **1817** and founded the **Vedanta College** in **1825**.

questions.question: Which of the following is/are example(s) of an abiotic factor in an ecosystem?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Soil**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• An **ecosystem** is composed of two major components: **Biotic factors** (living components) and **Abiotic factors** (non-living components).
 
• **Soil** is a critical **abiotic factor** as it is a **non-living** substance consisting of **minerals**, **organic matter**, **gases**, **liquids**, and countless organisms that together support life on **Earth**. It provides **nutrients** and **physical support** for plants. ***Hence, Soil is the correct answer.***
 
• **Bacteria** are **unicellular microorganisms** that are considered **living organisms**. In an ecosystem, they often function as **decomposers** or **pathogens**, making them a **biotic factor**. ***Hence, Bacteria is an incorrect statement.***
 
• **Insects** are **multicellular organisms** belonging to the **Animalia** kingdom. They are **living beings** that interact with their environment as **pollinators**, **consumers**, or **prey**, which classifies them as **biotic factors**. ***Hence, Insects is an incorrect statement.***
 
• **Trees** are **perennial plants** that are **living organisms**. They act as **primary producers** in many ecosystems by converting **solar energy** into **chemical energy** through **photosynthesis**, thus they are **biotic factors**. ***Hence, Trees is an incorrect statement.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Abiotic Factors:** These refer to the **non-living physical and chemical elements** in the **ecosystem**. Abiotic resources are usually obtained from the **lithosphere**, **atmosphere**, and **hydrosphere**.

 
 
• **Sunlight:** The ultimate **source of energy** for life on **Earth**. It governs the **temperature** and drives **photosynthesis**.
 
• **Water:** A vital **abiotic component** required for **biochemical reactions** within living cells. Its **availability** determines the type of **ecosystem** (e.g., **desert** vs. **rainforest**).
 
• **Temperature:** Influences the **metabolic rates** of organisms. Most life forms are adapted to survive within a specific **temperature range**.
 
• **Atmosphere:** Provides **Oxygen** for **respiration** and **Carbon Dioxide** for **photosynthesis**.
 
 
 
• **Biotic Factors:** These are the **living parts** of an ecosystem, which include **animals**, **plants**, **fungi**, and **bacteria**.
 
 
• **Producers (Autotrophs):** Organisms like **green plants** and **algae** that produce their own food.
 
• **Consumers (Heterotrophs):** Organisms that depend on others for food, such as **herbivores**, **carnivores**, and **omnivores**.
 
• **Decomposers (Saprotrophs):** Organisms like **fungi** and **bacteria** that break down **dead organic matter**, recycling **nutrients** back into the **soil**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Interdependence:** Biotic and abiotic factors are **interrelated**. If one factor is altered or removed, it can affect the entire **ecosystem**. For example, a change in **soil pH** (abiotic) can prevent certain **plants** (biotic) from growing.
 
• **Limiting Factors:** Any **abiotic factor** that restricts the **numbers**, **reproduction**, or **distribution** of organisms is called a **limiting factor**. Common examples include **scarcity of water** in **arid regions** or **low sunlight** in the **deep ocean**.
 
• **Location-specific Factors:** The importance of specific abiotic factors can vary by **location**. In **marine ecosystems**, **salinity** and **water pressure** are key factors, whereas in **terrestrial ecosystems**, **soil composition** and **altitude** are more significant.
